questions.q: What does NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) describe, and how does SQL Server handle it by default?
options: Multi-socket servers where each CPU has faster access to its own local memory bank; SQL Server's scheduler is NUMA-aware by default, with no configuration required to enable it
A storage protocol used only by SSDs, unrelated to CPU or memory architecture
A licensing model that charges per NUMA node instead of per core
A SQL Server feature that must be manually enabled via sp_configure before it has any effect
questions.explain: NUMA is a hardware memory-locality architecture, and SQL Server's scheduler already accounts for it automatically, without any setting to turn on.

questions.q: Why does this lesson emphasize storage latency over throughput (MB/sec or IOPS) for OLTP workloads?
options: OLTP workloads do many small, random reads and writes, and latency per I/O — not raw throughput — is what actually predicts user-visible pain
Throughput is irrelevant to all SQL Server workloads, OLTP or otherwise
Latency and throughput always move together, so either number tells you the same thing
Storage vendors never publish latency specifications, only throughput
questions.explain: For small, random OLTP I/O patterns, how long each individual request takes to complete matters more than the storage's advertised bulk throughput.

questions.q: What does a high AVERAGE wait time per wait on PAGEIOLATCH_SH specifically indicate, per this lesson?
options: A real sign that the underlying storage's actual latency, not just its labeled throughput, is the bottleneck
That the query is CPU-bound rather than I/O-bound
That statistics are out of date and need updating
That the buffer pool is oversized and should be reduced
questions.explain: A high average wait time per individual PAGEIOLATCH wait points specifically at slow storage latency as the bottleneck, as distinct from just a high total wait time.

questions.q: What is soft-NUMA, as described in this lesson?
options: A configuration that splits one large physical NUMA node into multiple smaller logical nodes, useful on servers with very high core counts and heavy tempdb/latch contention
A software emulation of NUMA on servers that have only a single physical CPU socket
The default (and only) way SQL Server schedules threads on any server
A trace flag that disables NUMA awareness entirely
questions.explain: Soft-NUMA is a real, narrow tuning lever for spreading scheduling and contention across more, smaller logical nodes on high-core-count servers.

questions.q: What is the real tradeoff this lesson describes between CPU core count and SQL Server licensing?
options: More cores mean more potential parallel capacity, but SQL Server's per-core licensing makes every additional core a direct, ongoing cost — the decision should be based on measured parallel headroom, not an assumption that more cores is always better
SQL Server licensing is unaffected by core count on any edition
Adding cores always reduces licensing cost because fewer servers are needed
CPU core count has no effect on query performance, only on licensing cost
questions.explain: Because licensing scales with core count, the decision to add cores should be justified by measured wait-stats evidence of real parallel headroom, not assumed.
